items.followUp: Define nuclear chemistry, inorganic chemistry, and geochemistry.

rubric.why: Defines physical chemistry.
rubric.how: Award the mark for explaining that it studies the physical properties and physical changes of matter, or the energy changes involved in chemical reactions.

rubric.why: Defines organic chemistry.
rubric.how: Award the mark for identifying it as the study of carbon compounds.

rubric.why: Defines biochemistry.
rubric.how: Award the mark for explaining that it studies chemical substances or processes in living organisms.

rubric.why: Defines industrial chemistry.
rubric.how: Award the mark for relating it to the manufacture or industrial production of chemicals.

rubric.why: Defines environmental chemistry.
rubric.how: Award the mark for explaining that it studies chemical processes in the environment, including the effects of pollutants.

modelAnswer: Physical Chemistry: The branch of chemistry that studies the physical properties of matter and the physical changes it undergoes.
Organic Chemistry: The branch of chemistry that studies carbon compounds.
Bio Chemistry: The branch of chemistry that studies the chemical substances and processes in living organisms.
Industrial Chemistry: The branch of chemistry concerned with the manufacture of chemicals and the processes used in chemical industries.
Environmental Chemistry: The branch of chemistry that studies chemical processes in the environment and the effects of pollutants.

items.followUp: Write any four postulates of Dalton’s atomic theory.

rubric.why: Identifies the permitted stationary orbits.
rubric.how: Award the mark for stating that electrons revolve around the nucleus in fixed, permitted orbits or energy levels.

rubric.why: States that electrons do not radiate energy in permitted orbits.
rubric.description: No radiation in a stationary orbit
rubric.how: Award the mark for stating that an electron in a permitted stationary orbit neither emits nor absorbs energy.

rubric.why: States Bohr’s quantization condition.
rubric.how: Award the mark for giving the condition mvr = nh/2π, or explaining that angular momentum is quantized.

rubric.why: Explains energy changes when electrons move between orbits.
rubric.description: Energy emitted or absorbed during a transition
rubric.how: Award the mark for stating that an electron emits or absorbs energy when it jumps between energy levels, with ΔE = hν as an acceptable expression.

modelAnswer: Electrons revolve around the nucleus in certain fixed circular orbits, called energy levels.
An electron in a permitted stationary orbit does not emit or absorb energy.
The angular momentum of an electron in an allowed orbit is quantized: mvr = nh/2π.
An electron emits or absorbs energy only when it jumps from one energy level to another; the energy change is ΔE = hν.

items.followUp: State five physical properties of non-metals.

rubric.why: Identifies the lustre of metals.
rubric.how: Award the mark for stating that metals have a shiny surface or are lustrous.

rubric.why: Identifies the ability of metals to be shaped into sheets.
rubric.how: Award the mark for stating that metals can be beaten or hammered into thin sheets.

rubric.why: Identifies the ability of metals to be drawn into wires.
rubric.how: Award the mark for stating that metals can be drawn into wires.

rubric.why: Identifies electrical conductivity.
rubric.how: Award the mark for stating that metals conduct electricity well.

rubric.why: Identifies thermal conductivity.
rubric.how: Award the mark for stating that metals conduct heat well.

modelAnswer: Metals are generally lustrous (shiny).
They are malleable and can be hammered into thin sheets.
They are ductile and can be drawn into wires.
They are good conductors of electricity.
They are good conductors of heat.

items.followUp: Define melting point and explain how pressure and impurities can affect it.

rubric.why: Gives the definition of boiling point.
rubric.how: Award the mark for stating that the boiling point is the temperature at which a liquid’s vapour pressure equals the external pressure.

rubric.why: Explains the effect of external pressure.
rubric.how: Award the mark for explaining that increasing external pressure raises the boiling point and decreasing it lowers the boiling point.

rubric.why: Explains how dissolved impurities affect boiling point.
rubric.how: Award the mark for stating that non-volatile impurities generally raise the boiling point.

rubric.why: Explains the effect of the nature of the liquid.
rubric.how: Award the mark for relating boiling point to intermolecular forces: stronger attractions require more energy and give a higher boiling point.

modelAnswer: The boiling point of a liquid is the temperature at which its vapour pressure becomes equal to the external pressure.
External pressure: Increasing the pressure raises the boiling point; decreasing the pressure lowers it.
Impurities: Dissolved non-volatile impurities generally raise the boiling point.
Nature of the liquid: Stronger intermolecular forces require more energy to overcome and result in a higher boiling point.

items.followUp: Compare a suspension and a colloid using four properties.

rubric.why: Compares the apparent nature of the mixtures.
rubric.how: Award the mark for identifying a solution as homogeneous and a colloid as heterogeneous, though it may appear homogeneous.

rubric.why: Compares particle sizes.
rubric.how: Award the mark for stating that solution particles are smaller than colloidal particles; typical ranges are below 1 nm for solutions and about 1–1000 nm for colloids.

rubric.why: Distinguishes the mixtures by the Tyndall effect.
rubric.how: Award the mark for stating that solutions do not show the Tyndall effect, whereas colloids do.

rubric.why: Compares passage through ordinary filter paper.
rubric.how: Award the mark for stating that particles of both solutions and colloids pass through ordinary filter paper.

rubric.why: Compares the stability of dispersed particles.
rubric.how: Award the mark for stating that solution particles and colloidal particles do not settle on standing.

modelAnswer: A solution is homogeneous, whereas a colloid is heterogeneous but may appear homogeneous.
Solution particles are smaller than 1 nm; colloidal particles are about 1–1000 nm in size.
A solution does not show the Tyndall effect; a colloid scatters light and shows the Tyndall effect.
Particles of both solutions and colloids pass through ordinary filter paper.
Particles in both mixtures remain dispersed and do not settle on standing.

items.followUp: Write the conditions necessary for rusting and the balanced equation for the formation of rust.

rubric.why: Identifies the conditions needed for rusting.
rubric.how: Award the mark for stating that rusting requires iron, oxygen, and water or moisture.

rubric.why: Describes oxidation of iron at the anode.
rubric.how: Award the mark for showing or describing iron losing electrons to form iron(II) ions: Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻.

rubric.why: Shows formation of hydroxide intermediates.
rubric.how: Award the mark for explaining that oxygen and water produce hydroxide ions, which react with iron ions to form iron hydroxides.

rubric.why: Identifies the final rust product.
rubric.how: Award the mark for identifying rust as hydrated iron(III) oxide, Fe₂O₃·xH₂O, or giving the balanced overall equation.

modelAnswer: Rusting occurs when iron is exposed to both oxygen and water (moisture).
At the anode, iron is oxidized: Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻.
Oxygen and water form hydroxide ions; these combine with Fe²⁺ ions to form iron(II) hydroxide, Fe(OH)₂, which is further oxidized to iron(III) hydroxide, Fe(OH)₃.
The iron(III) hydroxide forms hydrated iron(III) oxide (rust), Fe₂O₃·xH₂O; overall: 4Fe + 3O₂ + 2xH₂O → 2Fe₂O₃·xH₂O.

items.followUp: Define qualitative analysis and state what it determines.

rubric.why: States that analytical chemistry identifies components of matter.
rubric.how: Award the mark for explaining that analytical chemistry identifies the components or substances present in a sample.

rubric.why: States that analytical chemistry determines composition or amounts.
rubric.how: Award the mark for explaining that it determines the composition or amounts of the components in a sample.

modelAnswer: Analytical chemistry is the branch of chemistry concerned with separating, identifying, and determining the composition or amounts of the components of a substance.

items.followUp: How many moles are present in 49 g of sulphuric acid (H₂SO₄)?

rubric.why: Calculates the molar mass of phosphoric acid.
rubric.how: Award the mark for obtaining M(H₃PO₄) = 98 g mol⁻¹ (0.098 kg mol⁻¹).

rubric.why: Uses the mole formula correctly and gives the result with its unit.
rubric.how: Award the mark for substituting in n = m/M and obtaining approximately 0.408 mol.

modelAnswer: Given: m = 40 g = 0.040 kg.
Formula: n = m/M.
Substitution: n = 0.040 kg ÷ 0.098 kg mol⁻¹ = 0.408 mol.
Answer: 0.408 mol of H₃PO₄.
